title: Not a Single Thought Arises, Yet All Is Distinctly Clear
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: Is "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear" a good state or a bad state? Why do some Chan masters scold this state so severely?

inline.s: Question: Is "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear" a good state or a bad state? Why do some Chan masters scold this state so severely?

Answer: Chan meditation can be divided into four stages: 1. The myriad thoughts return to one — only the single thought of the huatou (the critical phrase) remains; 2. The one returns to nothing — even the single thought of the huatou is gone,
and at this time the practice is to investigate, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, back to the point before a single thought has arisen

; 3. Seeing the nature and awakening to the mind (enlightenment); 4. Doing the work of protecting and nurturing, merging mind and object in the awakening, purifying the flowing consciousness of present karma, so that deluded thoughts and emotional cogitations are all melted into the single flavor of the true mind.

Now "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear" is precisely the stage of "the one returning to nothing." For a person who has not yet reached single-mindedness without confusion, or who has only a preliminary stage of it, this is a good state. However, for a person who has already reached "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear," if he clings to this state as final, letting go of the doubt-sensation and ceasing to investigate, then he is utterly and completely wrong. Those who scold this state are not actually saying that the state itself is bad, but that one must on no account cling to it as final, because there still remain the two great stages of seeing the nature and of protecting and nurturing.
The Venerable Xuyun teaches:
"There are some
(some people)

who, because they have reached this state and have some slight mastery of the practice, and have not met any state they could not break through, think that ignorance has been utterly cut off and their practice is complete. Little do they know that they are living day after day in the cave of ignorance without realizing it. The moment they meet a state they cannot break through, they lose their mastery and are carried away by it as before — is this not a pity! Or there are some who, having reached the state where the genuine doubt-sensation appears before them, develop a little wisdom in the void and grasp a few of the ancients' public cases,
and then let go of the doubt-sensation

(to let go of the doubt-sensation at this point is to enter a wrong path; one should continue to practice diligently and unceasingly, investigating back to the point before a single thought has arisen, and never rest until one has seen the nature and awakened to the mind)

, imagining that they have attained great and thorough enlightenment, composing poems and verses, winking their eyes and raising their brows, and calling themselves good spiritual friends. Such people deceive themselves and deceive others, and their offenses are boundless. There are still others who misinterpret Bodhidharma's words 'outwardly cease all conditions, inwardly let the mind not pant, with the mind like a wall, one may enter the Way,' and the Sixth Patriarch's words 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, just at this very
nèn
moment, which is your original face, Acarya Ming?' — and so they take sitting by the withered tree as the ultimate.
Such people take the conjured city for the place of treasure, and mistake a lodging place for their homeland; the old woman burning the hermitage is precisely a scolding of such dead men.
(For details, see
the Chan Teachings of Xuyun
[doubt-sensation] The state of investigating without thought is called the doubt-sensation. [
to let go of the doubt-sensation at this point,

that is to enter a wrong path] At this time everything is pure and clear, with boundless ease; if one slightly loses the doubt-sensation (slightly loses the "investigating"), it becomes the state of no-memory, which the Chan communities call "the withered tree" and "a stone soaked in cold water" — how much more so if one regards it as final and deliberately lets go of the doubt-sensation! An ancient worthy said:
"Before the withered tree there are many forking paths; travelers arriving here all waste their time."

[misinterpreting the meaning] 1. In Bodhidharma's teaching "outwardly cease all conditions, inwardly let the mind not pant, with the mind like a wall, one may enter the Way," the phrase "one may enter the Way" means: one may begin to realize the Way — that is, having accomplished the first three phrases, one has completed the preparatory work before realizing the Way. But some people mistakenly think that accomplishing "outwardly cease all conditions, inwardly let the mind not pant, with the mind like a wall" is itself the realization of the Way, the final attainment. 2. In the Sixth Patriarch's teaching "not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, just at this very moment, which is your original face, Acarya Ming?," the word "na ge" (which) has the meaning of "which one" in modern Chinese (in the ancient language there was no separate character for "which"; the character "na" had two meanings — one is the modern "that," the other the modern "which"), and not the modern meaning of "that one." Yet some people mistakenly take "na ge is your original face, Acarya Ming" to mean, expressed in modern Chinese: that (That) is your original face. Hence they mistakenly think that "not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, just at this very moment" is itself the original face.

[conjured city] an illusory city. This is the parable of the conjured city in the Lotus Sutra. The place where all living beings attain Buddhahood is the place of treasure, but the road to it is perilous and long. Fearing that travelers would grow weary and turn back, the Buddha conjured a city midway so that they might rest a while, gather their strength, and then press on to the place of treasure. The Buddha wishes all living beings to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, but because living beings are faint-hearted and weak, unable to bear the burden, he first taught the Hinayana nirvana, so that they might attain this nirvana as a temporary resting place, and from there arouse the greater resolve and advance toward the true place of treasure, the Mahayana nirvana (the fruit of Buddhahood).

[the old woman burning the hermitage] A Chan public case: Long ago an old woman supported a hermit for twenty years, always sending a young girl to serve him his meals. One day the old woman had the girl embrace him and ask: "How do you feel right now?" The hermit said: "A withered tree leaning on a cold cliff, with no warmth even in midwinter." The girl reported these words to the old woman. The old woman said: "For twenty years I have only supported a worldly fellow (an unenlightened ordinary man)." And she drove him away and burned the thatched hermitage. This public case shows that the hermit took the conjured city for the place of treasure (thinking the state of no-thought to be final), able to die but not to live. (See the Wudeng Huiyuan, the Five Lamps Merged.) Chan Master Daoyuan
wrote a verse
"The man sitting still atop the hundred-foot pole
not a single thought arising
, though he has entered, is not yet genuine
not final
; atop the hundred-foot pole he must take a further step
thoroughly see his original nature
, and the worlds of the ten directions are his whole body."
(Jingde Chuandeng Lu, the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
Master Hanshan teaches:
"This matter
(the single road upward)
— if one does not lay down body and mind and keenly
investigate to the root

until the water is exhausted and the mountains end, there will never be a final resolution. Even when one reaches the point where the water is exhausted and the mountains end, the ancients called this the dead water of still
(here "chen" is the same as "sink")

sinking, and also called it the den of the mysterious and wondrous. If one does not turn one's head around, then what lies before is like an iron wall and silver mountain: it is only a place of gaining strength, not a place of true enjoyment. The way the ancients applied their minds was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must bring forth life from within death, and the essential lies in turning the pivot and shifting the position. Hence it is said: 'The man sitting atop the hundred-foot pole, though he has entered, is not yet genuine; atop the hundred-foot pole take a further step, and the great chiliocosm appears as his whole body.'"
(Mengyou ji,
"Instruction to Chan Practitioner Zhuanyu Heng"; for the commentary see
the Record of Master Hanshan's Teachings
in the section "Illnesses of the Body and Illnesses of Chan")

Therefore, "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear" still has a long stretch of road ahead for one who wishes to be free of birth and death by self-power. If one clings to it as final, one will surely fall into the cycle of birth and death, and so it deserves a shout or a blow on the head! But if one practices Chan and Pure Land together, and attains "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear," then even if one cannot see the nature and awaken to the mind in this life, at the moment of death one will surely be born in the highest grade of the highest birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and be free of birth and death. Master Hanshan gives a clear teaching on this — for details, see
the Instructions on Investigative Buddha-Recitation
Question: Does "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear" mean that no thoughts at all remain?

Answer: The "not a single thought arising" spoken of here means that there is only the doubt-sensation of investigating back to the point before a single thought has arisen, with no huatou and no other thoughts. "Yet all distinctly clear" means that one clearly and distinctly knows that one is "investigating," and that there is no other thought. In fact, this "investigating" is itself also a thought, but it is the key to seeing the nature, and it is extremely precious. When only the single thought of "investigating back to the point before a single thought has arisen" remains, that is the genuine doubt-sensation appearing before one. Practice this over a long time, and the single thought of "investigating" will suddenly snap; mind and object will both perish, and one sees the nature and awakens to the mind.
[mind and object both perish] the investigating mind and the investigated object are extinguished together — subject and object both perish.

To sum up, the conclusion is: when one reaches the stage of "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear," one must not cling to it as final, but must continue to practice diligently and unceasingly, investigating back to the point before a single thought has arisen, and take a further step atop the hundred-foot pole. At the same time, one should practice Chan and Pure Land together, to ensure being free of birth and death in this life. In this way, "not a single thought arising, yet all distinctly clear" is an extremely good state.
